II.1.title: The pole star
II.1.reflection: A ruler who governs by virtue is like the pole star: it stays in its place and the other stars turn around it. The image is of influence without force. The ruler does not chase anything; others orient themselves by him.
II.1.question: Is there someone whose steadiness, more than anything they said, set the direction for people around them?

II.2.title: No crooked thoughts
II.2.reflection: Confucius sums up the three hundred poems of the Book of Odes in one phrase from one of them: no depraved thoughts, or thoughts that do not swerve. Whatever the poems are about, love, war, complaint, they are honest. The summary is about the spirit of the collection, not its subject matter.
II.2.question: What book, song or poem would you sum up in a single line, and which line?

II.3.title: Laws and shame
II.3.reflection: Lead people by laws and keep them in line with punishments, and they will try to escape the punishment and feel no shame. Lead them by virtue and ritual, and they will have a sense of shame and set themselves right. The chapter is the book's clearest statement of how it thinks order is made.
II.3.question: In your own experience, has a rule or the example of a person done more to change how you behave?

II.4.title: From fifteen to seventy
II.4.reflection: The Master's life in six stages: at fifteen set on learning, at thirty standing firm, at forty without doubts, at fifty knowing the decrees of Heaven, at sixty with an ear attuned, at seventy following his heart without overstepping. It is the only autobiography the book gives him, and it describes a long ripening rather than a single conversion.
II.4.question: If you had to name the stage you are in now, what would you call it?
II.4.exercise: Write one line for each decade of your life so far, saying what you were set on then.

II.5.title: Not disobeying
II.5.reflection: Meng Yi asks about filial piety and is told "not disobeying". Later, in the carriage, Confucius explains to Fan Chi what he meant: serve parents by ritual while they live, bury them by ritual, sacrifice to them by ritual. Meng Yi belonged to one of the great families that used rites above their station, so "not disobeying" may have meant not disobeying ritual itself.
II.5.question: Have you ever given a short answer that only made sense once you explained it to someone else?

II.6.title: Parents' worry
II.6.reflection: Asked about filial piety by Meng Wu, Confucius answers with a sentence about parents: they worry that their children will fall ill. The line can be read two ways: give them nothing else to worry about, or know that this worry is how they love you. The chapter leaves both open.
II.6.question: Which reading of this chapter seems truer to you, and why?

II.7.title: More than feeding
II.7.reflection: To Ziyou, Confucius says that filial piety nowadays means supporting one's parents, but even dogs and horses are fed. Without reverence, what makes the difference? The point is not the provision but the attitude in which it is given.
II.7.question: What is the difference, for you, between looking after someone and respecting them?

II.8.title: The difficulty is the face
II.8.reflection: To Zixia, the answer is that the hard part is one's countenance. Doing the work for elders and serving them food and wine first is not yet the thing itself. The expression with which it is done tells more than the doing.
II.8.question: Does your face, when you help someone, say the same as your hands?

II.9.title: Hui is not stupid
II.9.reflection: Yan Hui listens all day without objecting, and Confucius wonders whether he is slow. Then he watches how Hui lives on his own and finds that he carries out everything he heard. Silence in a student, the chapter suggests, is not always absence of thought.
II.9.question: Whom have you misjudged as dull because they did not argue?

II.10.title: See, mark, examine
II.10.reflection: Three ways to know a person: look at what they do, observe how they do it and why, and see where they find their rest. Then, twice, how can a person hide? The repetition sounds like a teacher who has watched people for many years.
II.10.question: Where do you find your rest, and what would it tell an observer about you?

II.11.title: Old and new
II.11.reflection: Keep warming up what you already know and come to know what is new, and you can be a teacher. The verb in the Chinese suggests reheating. Old knowledge is not a store to be kept but something to be brought back to warmth again and again.
II.11.question: What old piece of knowledge have you not revisited in years?

II.12.title: Not a utensil
II.12.reflection: The junzi, Legge's "accomplished scholar" here, is not a vessel, not a tool made for a single use. A person of worth is not defined by one function. This six-word chapter is often quoted against narrow specialisation, though its first sense is about character, not careers.
II.12.question: Is there a part of you that has been made into a single-purpose tool?

II.13.title: Act first, then speak
II.13.reflection: Zigong, who was a gifted talker, asks about the junzi. He is told: such a person acts first and then speaks in accordance with the action. The answer is fitted to the asker.
II.13.question: What have you said you would do that you have not yet done?

II.14.title: Catholic, not partisan
II.14.reflection: The junzi is broad in sympathy and does not form cliques; the small man forms cliques and is not broad. Legge's "catholic" means universal, the nineteenth-century sense of the word. The contrast between the junzi and the small man runs through the whole book.
II.14.question: Where do you find yourself taking a side before you have considered the matter?

II.15.title: Learning and thinking
II.15.reflection: Learning without thought is lost labour; thinking without learning is dangerous. Each needs the other. The chapter refuses both the student who memorises and the thinker who never reads.
II.15.question: Which of the two do you lean toward, learning or thinking?

II.16.title: Strange doctrines
II.16.reflection: Legge reads this as a warning against studying heterodox doctrines. Other translators read the same words as "attacking the other end" or "working on the wrong end", which would make it a warning about method rather than about rival schools. The short chapter has been argued over for two thousand years.
II.16.question: How do you decide which ideas are worth your attention, and which only distract?

II.17.title: What knowledge is
II.17.reflection: To Zilu, the confident one, Confucius explains: when you know something, hold that you know it; when you do not, admit that you do not. That is knowledge. It is the most quoted definition in the book, and it is also a gentle correction of the person it was addressed to.
II.17.question: What do you claim to know that you would have to admit you do not?
II.17.exercise: Once today, when asked something you are unsure of, say plainly that you do not know.

II.18.title: Few regrets
II.18.reflection: Zizhang is studying with an eye on an official salary. Confucius does not scold him; he tells him how: hear much, leave aside what is doubtful, speak carefully of the rest; see much, leave aside what is risky, act carefully on the rest. With few mistakes in speech and few regrets in conduct, a salary follows.
II.18.question: What would you set aside as doubtful before you speak today?

II.19.title: Raise the straight
II.19.reflection: Duke Ai of Lu asks how to win the people's obedience. Raise the upright and set them over the crooked, and the people will follow; do the reverse, and they will not. The answer is about whom a ruler promotes, which the people can see.
II.19.question: In a group you belong to, who gets raised, and what does that teach everyone else?

II.20.title: Gravity, care, example
II.20.reflection: Ji Kangzi, the most powerful man in Lu, asks how to make the people respectful, loyal and eager. Each answer turns the question back to him: be dignified and they will respect you; be filial and kind and they will be loyal; promote the good and teach the unable and they will be eager. The ruler is asked to change himself.
II.20.question: What do you ask of others that you have not first asked of yourself?

II.21.title: Government at home
II.21.reflection: Someone asks why Confucius does not take part in government. He quotes the Book of Documents on being filial and brotherly, and says that this too is government. Ordering a household is part of ordering the world. The answer also explains, without complaint, why he is out of office.
II.21.question: What counts as public work that is usually not counted?

II.22.title: The yoke-pin
II.22.reflection: A person without good faith is like a cart without the pin that joins the yoke to the shaft: it cannot move. The image is a small, essential piece of wood. Trust is not decoration; without it nothing goes anywhere.
II.22.question: What small promise, broken, would stop something larger from moving?

II.23.title: Ten generations ahead
II.23.reflection: Zizhang asks whether the future can be known. Confucius answers from history: the Yin took over the rites of the Xia, the Zhou those of the Yin, and what each added and removed can be known. So even a hundred generations on can be known. He reads the future as continuity in ritual, not as prediction.
II.23.question: What in your own life has been carried forward from your parents' time, and what has been changed?

II.24.title: Courage and flattery
II.24.reflection: Two sentences put side by side. Sacrificing to spirits that are not one's own is flattery. Seeing what is right and not doing it is a lack of courage. One is doing what one should not, the other not doing what one should.
II.24.question: What have you seen to be right recently and not done?
